title: The Harvard study
hookLine: the Harvard Study of Adult Development, following the same lives for decades, found close relationships predicted health and happiness

cards: Ask a room of young adults what will make their lives go well, and the answers come quickly: money, a good job, maybe being known for something. Now ask a different question. What if someone actually checked?
Followed a group of people from youth into old age, asked about their work, health, marriages, friends and worries, again and again, and then looked at who flourished?
Researchers at Harvard did just that, and the headline finding comes down to one word.

teach.b: The Harvard Study of Adult Development began with two groups of young men: students at Harvard, and boys from poorer neighborhoods of Boston.
Researchers followed them for decades, through jobs, wars, marriages, illness and old age, and later went on to study their children.
When the current director, the psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, sums it up, the headline isn't wealth or fame. It's relationships.
People with warm, close ties to family, friends and community were, on the whole, happier and healthier as they aged.
How satisfied people were in their relationships in midlife went on to predict their health years later.
It's quality, not count. Waldinger points out that a person can be lonely in a crowd, or in a marriage, and that high-conflict relationships seem to wear people down.
What mattered was having people you could truly count on.
In their book The Good Life, Waldinger and his co-author, Marc Schulz, compare relationships to fitness: they weaken when neglected and grow with steady care.
Ecclesiastes puts the stakes of having no one plainly: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."
One honest caution: a study like this shows what goes together. It can't by itself prove what causes what.

how: The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed its participants, and later their children, through regular questionnaires, interviews and medical checks; its directors summarize its findings for the public as evidence that close relationships matter for health and happiness.

games.q: a friendship that matters has gone quiet. no fight, just drift. by today's findings, what helps?
o: wait for them to reach out first.
one small act of upkeep: a message, a walk, a question.
make a lot of new friends instead.
games.why: Waldinger and Schulz compare relationships to fitness: they weaken when neglected and grow with steady care.

practice: Bring to mind the few people you could call at three in the morning, and picture each one for a breath or two.

Then choose one relationship that matters to you and has gone a little quiet, not a fight, just drift, and imagine one small act of upkeep, a message, a walk, a question you've been meaning to ask: not the whole friendship, just the next small step.

wordCard.voice: Waldinger. The psychiatrist who directs the decades-long Harvard study and sums up its finding in one word: relationships. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: relationships. Like fitness, they weaken when neglected and grow with steady care. Day eight hundred fifty-three.
